title: The Year of Sorrow
subtitle: The Loss of Abu Talib and Khadijah, and the Trial of Makkan Hostility
summary: The physical exhaustion following the boycott, the passing of Abu Talib, the heartbreaking death of Khadijah رضي الله عنها, the deep personal grief of the Prophet ﷺ, the collapse of clan protection, and the alarming escalation of direct persecution in Makkah.

sections.text: The Heavy Toll of the Siege

Though Banu Hashim emerged victorious from the mountain pass after the nullification of the boycott, the three years of starvation, exposure to desert elements, and profound stress had taken an irreversible physical toll. In the tenth year of Prophethood, barely months after the cessation of the siege, the fragile health of the clan's venerable patriarch, Abu Talib, began to fail precipitously. He was now over eighty years of age, his body worn thin by the deprivations he had willingly shared with his nephew.

For over four decades, ever since the death of Abd al-Muttalib, Abu Talib had served as Muhammad's guardian, father figure, and immovable political protector. Under the strict conventions of Arabian tribal law, it was Abu Talib's unwavering shield that had prevented the chieftains of Quraysh from executing the Prophet. Even when offered kingship, riches, or handsome youths in exchange for his nephew, Abu Talib had consistently rebuffed every demand, swearing never to surrender Muhammad ﷺ while his breath remained.
The quiet rocky landscapes of Makkah where the Prophet walked through seasons of profound sorrow.

As death drew near, the Prophet ﷺ entered his uncle's quarters, yearning with all his heart for the salvation of the man who had loved and sheltered him so faithfully. Classical Hadith collections, including Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, record that the Prophet sat beside the dying patriarch and pleaded gently: 'O my uncle, say: There is no deity worthy of worship except God (La ilaha illallah)—a word through which I will plead on your behalf before God.'

However, Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah sat nearby, watching intently. Sensing the moment, they intervened aggressively to play on the dying chief's aristocratic pride: 'Will you turn away from the ancestral religion of Abd al-Muttalib, O Abu Talib?' They continued pressing him until Abu Talib uttered his final words, choosing to die upon the tradition of his forefathers out of dread that Quraysh would brand his conversion an act of cowardice at the door of death. Heartbroken, the Prophet ﷺ mourned his beloved guardian with profound sorrow.

Barely had the tears dried from the funeral of Abu Talib when a second, even more devastating blow struck the household of the Prophet ﷺ. Only thirty to forty days later (or a few months according to differing classical reports), his beloved wife, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid رضي الله عنها, fell critically ill and departed this life at approximately sixty-five years of age.

Khadijah had been the Prophet's steadfast anchor for twenty-five years. She was the first human being to believe in his mission, the visionary who enveloped him in her mantle when he descended trembling from Cave Hira, and the unwavering confidante who spent her entire immense mercantile fortune to sustain the believers through poverty and siege. Never had she doubted his truthfulness, never had she scolded or reproached him, and in her presence, the Messenger of God had always found tranquil refuge from the insults of the world.

إِنِّي قَدْ رُزِقْتُ حُبَّهَا
'Indeed, I was nourished and gifted with her love.' — Prophet Muhammad ﷺ concerning Khadijah (Sahih Muslim)

Her unique spiritual station was immortalized in authentic Hadith. Imam al-Bukhari records that the Angel Jibril once descended to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of God, here is Khadijah approaching with a vessel of food or drink. When she arrives, convey to her peace from her Lord and from me, and give her the glad tidings of a palace of pearl in Paradise, wherein there is neither clamor nor toil.' Her passing left a void in his heart that no earthly companion could fill.
The solemn sanctuary of the ancient Kaaba where open hostility erupted against the Prophet following the loss of his protectors.

Early biographers designated this sorrowful period as 'Am al-Huzn' (The Year of Sorrow). The bereavement was not merely emotional; it transformed the practical political realities of Makkah overnight. With Abu Talib dead, leadership of the Banu Hashim clan devolved upon Abu Lahab. Hostile, petty, and contemptuous of the faith, Abu Lahab soon withdrew clan protection from the Prophet ﷺ, leaving him entirely vulnerable under Arabian customary law.

Deprived of both familial refuge and legal protection, the Prophet ﷺ faced an immediate escalation in physical abuse. Vulgar agitators who had previously feared Abu Talib's wrath now dared to assault him openly in the streets. Once, an insolent neighbor cast filth and dust over his head as he walked through Makkah. When he returned home, one of his young daughters wept as she washed the dirt from his hair. The Prophet gently consoled her, saying: 'Do not weep, my daughter, for indeed God will protect your father.'

The Prophet ﷺ remarked with heavy heart: 'Quraysh never inflicted upon me anything that I detested so much until Abu Talib passed away.' Makkah had become a fortress of closed doors and hostile stares. Yet in this darkest hour of isolation, the prophetic gaze turned outward beyond the mountains of his birthplace, seeking new horizons where the divine call might find fertile ground.
